In the 1990s, during negotiations on amending the ABM Treaty, Russians vehemently argued that a national missile defense system, once deployed could not be meaningfully limited without arms control agreements.125 They threatened asymmetrical response to thwart any perceived dangers to the Russian nuclear deterrent.126 Strobe Talbott, President Clinton’s chief negotiator, writes that Russians worried that once the architecture was in place, it could be expanded significantly within a short period.127 He recounts that the Russians, basing their position on a worst-case scenario, calculated that the United States may be able to use precision weaponry to disable 90 percent of the Russian deterrent.128
